planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in early spring in well-drained, rocky or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; this large shrub is native to dolomite and limestone bluffs, glade margins, and open woodland edges of the Ozark Plateau in Missouri, Arkansas, and eastern Oklahoma.

directions: Ozark mock orange forms a large, arching, multi-stemmed shrub clothed in finely hairy (pubescent) leaf undersides, which distinguish it from the smoother-leaved mock oranges grown as garden ornamentals. In late spring it produces clusters of intensely fragrant, four-petaled white flowers along the previous year's wood, drawing bees and other pollinators to the open woodland edges and rocky bluffs where it naturally grows. Once established on the thin, well-drained soils typical of its native Ozark dolomite glades and bluff woodlands, it is notably drought tolerant and requires little care. Prune only to remove old, unproductive canes right after flowering, since next year's blooms form on the current season's new growth.

planting.note: Scatter seed on bare soil in fall in rich, humus-laden woodland soil in partial to full shade; spring avens germinates readily after natural winter cold and self-sows freely once established in a woodland setting.

directions: Spring avens is an easily overlooked but widespread native of rich, mesic woods across the Ozark Plateau and lower Midwest, producing small, five-petaled, pale yellow flowers on wiry branched stems in early to mid spring, well before most woodland wildflowers finish blooming. The flowers give way to distinctive bur-like seed heads covered in hooked bristles that cling readily to fur and clothing, aiding its spread through the forest floor. As a low, unassuming filler plant, it works well tucked among trilliums, bloodroot, and other spring ephemerals in a naturalized woodland garden, filling gaps as larger neighbors go dormant. It tolerates the dry shade and leaf litter typical of mature deciduous woods and needs no supplemental care once established.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall directly onto thin, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; seed needs a period of winter cold to germinate, mimicking the exposed dolomite glades where this species grows wild.

directions: Trelease's larkspur is a true Ozark endemic, confined to dolomite and limestone glades, bald knobs, and the thin-soiled open woodlands fringing them in Missouri and Arkansas. In mid-spring it sends up branched spikes of pale blue-violet to nearly white flowers above finely divided foliage, then goes fully dormant by midsummer as its glade habitat bakes in the heat. It thrives in the lean, rocky, fast-draining soil typical of glade margins shaded intermittently by scattered cedar and oak, and resents being grown in rich, moisture-retentive garden beds. Best suited to a rock garden or glade-restoration planting that recreates its native thin-soil, dappled-light conditions, where it is essentially pest-free and long-lived once settled.

planting.note: Sow seed or plant divisions in spring in rich, humus-laden, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade; American beakgrain is one of the few ornamental grasses that actually prefers the deep shade of a mature deciduous forest floor.

directions: American beakgrain grows naturally in rich, mesic deciduous woods across the Ozark Plateau and eastern United States, forming neat, slowly spreading clumps of arching, bamboo-like foliage that stay a clean green through summer. Its flowers are inconspicuous, but by late summer the plant produces distinctive shiny, asymmetrical, beaked seeds that give the genus its name and add a subtle textural interest. Unlike many woodland grasses that spread aggressively by rhizome, it clumps politely, making it a well-behaved choice for a shaded native plant border or under mature trees where turfgrass struggles. It tolerates considerable root competition and dry shade once established, needing only an occasional spring cleanup of old foliage.

planting.note: Sow seed in spring directly onto consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; lanceleaf rose gentian needs the steady seepage moisture of a savanna or bog-edge site to establish well.

directions: Lanceleaf rose gentian grows naturally in wet longleaf pine savannas, flatwoods depressions, and bog margins along the Atlantic coastal plain from New Jersey south to Florida, where canopy gaps provide the dappled light it prefers. Despite its common name, the flowers are pure white rather than rose-colored, each with five narrow petals surrounding a small greenish-yellow star at the throat, carried in loose clusters atop slender, erect stems through much of summer. It depends on consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil and struggles if allowed to dry out between waterings. In the garden it pairs naturally with pitcher plants, sundews, and other savanna wetland species in a sunny bog garden or rain garden low spot.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Sow seed in fall onto consistently damp, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; yellow colicroot grows naturally in the seepage zones of longleaf pine savannas and needs steady moisture through germination and establishment.

directions: Yellow colicroot is native to damp longleaf pine savannas, seepage slopes, and flatwoods from the Carolinas to the Florida panhandle, where it forms a low rosette of grass-like leaves that sends up a single wandlike flower spike in spring. The small, bell-shaped flowers open bright yellow rather than the dull white typical of the more common Aletris farinosa, and the species favors noticeably wetter, more consistently seeping sites than its white-flowered relative. It makes a graceful vertical accent at the sunny to lightly shaded edge of a bog garden or savanna-style planting, where its moisture needs can be reliably met. Established clumps increase slowly and resent prolonged drying out, so site it where runoff or a high water table keeps the soil reliably damp.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Sow seed in spring onto consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; this low sneezeweed grows naturally in the shallow, seasonally wet ditches and depressions of pine savanna and flatwoods habitat.

directions: Savanna sneezeweed is a low, compact species of wet pine savannas, flatwoods ditches, and seepage bogs from South Carolina to Florida, easily told apart from the taller common sneezeweed by its deeply cut, feathery basal foliage. It blooms in early to mid spring, notably earlier than most other Helenium species, bearing cheerful yellow daisy-like flowers with drooping rays around a domed central disk. Its small stature and tolerance of consistently damp, sandy, acidic soil make it a good fit for the sunny to lightly shaded margin of a bog garden or rain garden rather than a conventional dry border. Established plants spread modestly and benefit from the same reliable moisture found in their native savanna seeps.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in acidic, sandy, humus-poor soil with reliable moisture in full sun to partial shade; Carolina wicky grows naturally at the damp margins of pine savannas and pocosins.

directions: Carolina wicky is a low evergreen shrub native to pine savannas, pocosin edges, and seasonally damp flatwoods of the Carolina and Georgia coastal plain, smaller and better adapted to warm, humid summers than its more northern relative, sheep laurel. In late spring, clusters of small, rose-pink, saucer-shaped flowers line the stems; like other kalmias, each flower holds its anthers under tension in small pockets that spring open to dust visiting bees with pollen. It performs best in acidic, sandy, nutrient-poor soil kept consistently moist, much like the savanna seepage zones where it naturally occurs, and resists most pests once established. As with all Kalmia species, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested, so site it away from grazing animals and curious pets.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Sow seed in spring onto consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; savanna honeycombhead grows naturally in the wet ditches and bog margins of longleaf pine savanna habitat.

directions: Savanna honeycombhead is native to wet pine savannas, bog margins, and roadside ditches of the coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and Louisiana, growing from a basal rosette of narrow leaves that largely withers away by bloom time. Wiry, mostly leafless stems rise through late summer and fall, each topped with a single bright yellow, daisy-like flowerhead whose domed, pitted center gives the genus its common name. It thrives in consistently moist, acidic, sandy soil in the full sun to lightly dappled light of a savanna canopy gap, and its tall, airy flowering stems add vertical late-season interest to a bog garden or wet meadow planting. Established clumps are long-lived but slow to bulk up, so give plants room and patience rather than frequent disturbance.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)
